title: Neural Collapse Inspired Debiased Representation Learning for Min-max Fairness

problem.claim: Group fairness methods can reduce performance for certain protected groups, producing sub-optimal outcomes; Min-max fairness instead prioritizes improvement for the worst-performing group.

gap.claim: Existing efforts to achieve Min-max fairness have limited effectiveness.

contributions.claim: The paper uses the Neural Collapse framework and a layer-peeled model to analyze ERM training by separating encoder representation learning from classifier learning.
The paper introduces a strategy with a frozen classifier to enhance representations directly and two easily implemented loss functions to guide learning.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors explicitly describe the frozen-classifier representation-enhancement strategy as novel.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Experiments on real-world benchmark datasets in Computer Vision, Natural Language Processing, and Tabular data report that the approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods for promoting Min-max fairness.

narrative_sequence.summary: Fairness is identified as a trustworthiness concern in real-world machine learning applications.
Common group fairness objectives may harm performance for some groups, while Min-max fairness prioritizes the worst-performing group but has limited existing effectiveness.
Neural Collapse and a layer-peeled model are used to examine ERM training and separate representation from classifier behavior.

Classifiers achieve maximum separation, but representations are insufficiently separable for minority groups; the authors attribute sub-optimal minority-group performance to representations rather than classifiers.
A frozen-classifier strategy and two loss functions are introduced, with benchmark experiments reported across three data domains.

source_observation.claim: The reported analysis links minority-group underperformance to insufficiently separable representations rather than insufficient classifier separation.

interpretation.claim: For worst-group performance, improving the learned representation may be more useful than modifying a classifier that already separates maximally.

application.claim: When addressing Min-max fairness, consider representation-focused interventions that preserve or freeze classifier behavior while guiding representation learning.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether this representation-focused strategy applies beyond the reported benchmark domains or under different fairness definitions.

unknowns: The benchmark dataset names, dataset sizes, and protected-group definitions are not specified.
The fairness and utility metrics, quantitative results, and statistical comparisons are not specified.
The two loss functions and training procedure are not described in detail.
The compared state-of-the-art methods are not identified.
